# Control narrative template for equipment modules

## 1. Principle: write behavior once, document only what is different

The 90% that is identical belongs in a **class narrative**, one per library type. Each pump or valve then gets a short **instance sheet** holding only tags, parameters, interlock sources and exceptions. Process sequencing (what calls the pump and when) lives in the unit or phase narrative, not in the equipment module.

| Level | Written | Content | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Class narrative | Once per library type and version | Modes, states, commands, standard faults, alarm behavior, HMI behavior | Standards owner, tied to the PLC library version |
| 2. Instance sheet | One per tag (generated from a table where possible) | Tag, I/O, scaling, setpoints, timers, interlock sources, alarm priorities, exceptions | Integrator, reviewed by the brewery |
| 3. Unit/phase narrative | Per process area | Who commands the module and when (e.g. CIP supply sequence) | Integrator |

Suggested classes for your platform (align the names with your actual library): `EM_Pump_DOL`, `EM_Pump_VFD`, `EM_Valve_OnOff` (with variants: single solenoid spring-return, double-acting, and with or without open/closed feedback). Mixproof and seat-lift valves should be separate classes if the library treats them separately.

## 2. Class narrative template (pump, VFD variant)

Each section is written once. Anything marked **[param]** is set on the instance sheet, never in the class text.

1. **Purpose and scope**: what the class covers, and the library block and version it describes.
2. **Modes**: Auto (commanded by unit/phase), Manual (operator from HMI, interlocks still active), Out of Service (module ignores commands, outputs off, alarms suppressed).
3. **Commands and setpoints**: Run request, speed setpoint (% or Hz), reset.
4. **Start permissives**: conditions required before starting. Class-level list: no active fault, drive ready, not Out of Service, plus **[param]** process permissives.
5. **Protective interlocks (trips)**: conditions that stop the pump while running. Class-level behavior: stop immediately, latch, require reset after the condition clears. The sources are **[param]**.
6. **Run feedback supervision**: start-confirmation timeout and unexpected-stop detection, with timers as **[param]**.
7. **Speed control**: ramp behavior, min/max limits **[param]**, behavior on loss of setpoint.
8. **Fault handling and reset**: drive fault, communication loss, feedback mismatch. Which faults latch, and what resets them.
9. **Fail-safe and power-up state**: output state on PLC stop, comms loss and power restore. The pump does not auto-restart unless stated.
10. **Alarms**: standard alarm list with default priorities. Instance-level changes go on the instance sheet.
11. **HMI**: faceplate behavior, what the operator can do in each mode.
12. **Runtime and maintenance data**: run hours, start count.
13. **Simulation and bypass rules**: whether interlocks can be bypassed, by whom, and how it is logged.

## 3. Instance sheet template (one per tag)

```
Tag / description:
Class and version:          (e.g. EM_Pump_VFD v__)
Area / unit:
Drive / MCC reference:
I/O and comms tags:         (run cmd, speed ref, run FB, drive fault, ready)
Speed limits:               min / max / default / ramp
Start permissives (beyond class):   source | condition | delay
Protective interlocks:              source | condition | delay | reset type
Alarms changed from default:        alarm | priority | setpoint | delay
Commanded by:               unit/phase references
Exceptions to class narrative:      "None" or numbered, each with reason
Open items / TBC:
```

The rule is that "Exceptions: None" is the normal entry. Every exception needs a reason and is tracked, so drift becomes visible rather than hidden in prose.

## 4. Valve class (short form)

The same structure applies: modes, open/close commands, position feedback and travel-time supervision, fail-safe position on air or power loss, fault latching, and alarms. The instance sheet holds the tag, I/O, travel timeout, fail position, and any interlock such as "do not open unless X". A table covers 300 valves well, since most rows differ only by tag and I/O.

## 5. Example: P-4021, CIP supply pump

Values below are **illustrative placeholders** I chose to show the format. They need to be confirmed against the actual process, drive and design data.

### Instance sheet: P-4021

| Field | Entry |
|---|---|
| Tag / description | P-4021, CIP supply pump |
| Class and version | EM_Pump_VFD, v__ (set to the project's library version) |
| Area / unit | CIP |
| Drive | VFD (drive tag/MCC ref: TBC) |
| I/O and comms | Run cmd, speed ref, run feedback, drive ready, drive fault: TBC per I/O list |
| Speed limits | Min 30% / Max 100% / Default 80% / Ramp 10 s up, 10 s down (placeholders) |
| Start permissives (beyond class) | PT-4022 suction pressure above low-low limit, or start-up bypass timer active (see below) |
| Protective interlock | **Dry-run protection**: see below |
| Alarms changed from default | PT-4022 low pressure: warning at 0.3 bar (placeholder); dry-run trip alarm priority High |
| Commanded by | CIP supply phase(s) in the CIP unit narrative: TBC references |
| Exceptions to class | None |
| Open items | Confirm PT-4022 location (suction side), range and limits; confirm retry policy |

### Dry-run protection (instance parameters, behavior from the class)

| Item | Entry |
|---|---|
| Source | PT-4022 |
| Condition | PT-4022 < low-low setpoint (0.15 bar, placeholder) |
| Start-up bypass | Condition ignored for 10 s after start to allow priming (placeholder) |
| Trip delay | Condition must persist 3 s while running (placeholder) |
| Action | Class-standard protective trip: stop pump, latch |
| Reset | Operator reset after PT-4022 is healthy again; no auto-restart |
| Instrument failure | PT-4022 bad quality or out of range is treated as a trip condition (confirm this is the wanted policy) |

### Narrative text in the project document

> **P-4021 CIP supply pump** is an instance of EM_Pump_VFD (see Class Narrative CN-PUMP-VFD, rev _). Its behavior is as described in that narrative except for the parameters and interlocks in the instance sheet above. Dry-run protection uses PT-4022 as described in the table. The pump is commanded by the CIP supply phases (see CIP Unit Narrative). **There are no exceptions to the class narrative.**

That is about half a page, versus a full copied paragraph per pump.

## 6. Rules to keep copies from drifting

1. **The class narrative has a version tied to the PLC library version.** Instance sheets cite it, and a library upgrade triggers a review of the narrative.
2. **No class behavior is restated in instance text.** Reviewers reject paragraphs that duplicate the class.
3. **Generate instance sheets from the I/O or equipment list** (spreadsheet or database to document) so tags and parameters are entered once.
4. **Exceptions are numbered and justified.** If the same exception appears on several tags, promote it to a new class variant.
5. **Contract it that way.** Specify the class narratives and instance-sheet format as the integrator's deliverable format. The brewery owns the class narratives, and the integrator proposes changes through the standards owner.
6. **Test from the same source.** Derive FAT/SAT checks per class once (modes, trips, resets), and per instance only the parameters and interlocks.

If you tell me the library's actual block names and the alarm philosophy, I can fill in the class narrative text itself, not just the headings.
